summary: Tamaulipas carries two documented deviations. Its legislature is among the six that have enacted no legal gender-recognition procedure at all (Human Rights Watch, March 2025), keeping trans people's documents permanently mismatched — the single most visitor-relevant legal fact in the country, since a mismatched document is what prompts a police check. And the country dossier names border Tamaulipas among the states where armed-group control amplifies trans-specific risk: armed groups and local police, not the penal code, decide how a gender-nonconforming person is treated, and both have documented patterns of extortion and sexual exploitation of trans women in detention.

NOTE: page not retrievable at fetch time; the underlying source is the Human Rights Watch report 'I Just Want to Contribute to Society' (6 March 2024) on the need for legal gender recognition in Tabasco, co-produced with the Centro Comunitario para la Inclusión, documenting that the absence of any recognition procedure leaves trans people exposed to police and institutional mistreatment.

The Guardian (24 July 2024): Mexico City's legislature approved the 'Paola Buenrostro law' making transfeminicide a distinct criminal offence, named for a trans woman murdered in 2016 whose killing remains unpunished; the report covers the vote and celebrants outside the congress building.

outOfScopeNotes: Blanket armed-group violence along the border affects every traveller regardless of gender expression; the trans-specific element is the documented targeting and extortion of trans women by those same actors, which the assessment covers.
